reference.source: Manson's Tropical Diseases / Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
clinicalPearls: Caused by Mycobacterium ulcerans, an environmental mycobacterium associated with slow-moving or stagnant water; most cases occur in West and Central Africa, with foci in Australia and elsewhere
The organism produces the toxin mycolactone, which causes tissue necrosis and local immunosuppression, explaining the characteristically painless lesion
Early disease presents as a painless nodule, plaque or oedematous area; without treatment it progresses to a painless ulcer with widely undermined edges
The undermined, deeply excavated ulcer with necrotic base extending beyond the visible skin margin is the hallmark of established disease
Diagnosis is confirmed by PCR for the IS2404 insertion sequence, supported by microscopy for acid-fast bacilli, culture and histopathology
Because lesions are painless, patients often present late with extensive tissue loss, and disease over joints can cause disabling contractures
Treatment combines prolonged rifampicin-based anti-mycobacterial therapy with wound care, and surgery or skin grafting for larger lesions; physiotherapy prevents contractures
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium ulcerans is acquired from aquatic environments, though the precise mode of transmission remains uncertain. Once in subcutaneous tissue it secretes mycolactone, a diffusible lipid toxin that induces coagulative necrosis of fat and dermis while suppressing local immune and pain responses, accounting for the painless, minimally inflamed lesion. Necrosis spreads laterally in the subcutaneous plane, producing ulcers whose undermined edges extend well beyond the surface defect. As anti-mycobacterial therapy reduces bacillary load, the local immunosuppressive effect lifts and healing can proceed, sometimes with a paradoxical inflammatory reaction.
additionalDifferentials: Squamous cell carcinoma (including within chronic ulcers)
Other mycobacterial or deep fungal infection
additionalInvestigations: PCR for the IS2404 sequence on swab or tissue (most sensitive confirmatory test)
Ziehl-Neelsen microscopy of swab or tissue for acid-fast bacilli
Culture of M. ulcerans (slow-growing, requires lower incubation temperature)
Histopathology showing necrosis with clumps of extracellular acid-fast bacilli
Imaging to assess deep or bone involvement in extensive disease
Assessment of functional impairment where lesions cross joints
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or oedematous lesions suggesting aggressive disease
Lesions crossing joints with impending contracture and disability
Malignant transformation in a long-standing chronic ulcer
Extensive tissue loss requiring reconstructive surgery
reference.prognosis: Early nodular disease can heal with antibiotics alone and minimal scarring, but late, extensive ulceration frequently leaves disfiguring scars, contractures and functional disability; relapse is uncommon with adequate combination therapy.
pitfalls: Attributing a painless chronic ulcer to trivial trauma and delaying diagnosis
Underestimating the true extent of necrosis, which extends beyond the visible ulcer margin
Relying on surgery alone without anti-mycobacterial therapy, risking recurrence
Missing malignant change in long-standing ulcers
references: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Give combination anti-mycobacterial therapy against Mycobacterium ulcerans, typically oral rifampicin with clarithromycin (or with an aminoglycoside such as streptomycin), as the mainstay that can heal early lesions without surgery
Provide wound care and dressings, with surgical debridement, excision and skin grafting for extensive or non-healing lesions
Anticipate and manage paradoxical inflammatory reactions that may occur during or after antibiotic treatment as bacillary load and mycolactone-driven immunosuppression fall
Deliver physiotherapy and contracture prevention for lesions crossing joints, with functional rehabilitation of established disability
Provide analgesia and treat secondary bacterial infection of ulcers
Monitor for relapse, which is uncommon with adequate combination therapy, and assess for deep or bone involvement in extensive disease
Refer to specialist or tropical medicine services and manage jointly with surgery and physiotherapy
